messages.subject: Debugging strategy: dump your environment.
messages.subject_clean: Debugging strategy: dump your environment.
messages.body_plain:
I apologize if this has been mentioned before. I don't think I have
seen this one written anywhere so thought I would mention.   I believe
this would work on a cluster with copyFiles=TRUE and some thought to
where files are going, though I debug on local so that is where it is
tested.

If you are familiar with debugger() in R you know that R errors arn't
actually R crashing or anything.  It is simply an activity that R goes
to when your script is nonsense (by whatever measure). One thing we
can do is tell R to save the environment when it gets to error in your
map/reduce code.  Since, the save the environment code is executed
before Rhipe's java gets any shot at the error the rest proceeds as
normal in map/reduce jobs.  Also, though we want to save the
environment to a unique file name so that if two mappers error at the
same time there is no nonsense to think about.

It loops like this in my code:

hloess.map = function(map.keys, map.values){
	old.error = options("error")
	options(error = function() save.image(paste("error.env",
map.keys[[1]],".RData",sep="")))
	<doing work>
	options(old.error)
}

If some where in <doing work> R chokes on an evaluation it executes a
save of the global environment image and then Rhipe takes over with
the error handling.  Now when we return to R we can (and I go to
another R instance for this step).  load the error.env.###.RData and
ls() the environment.  Eg in R load("error.env0.RData").  Usually it
is map.values *at the time of the error* that I immediately print out.

The value of operating in this way is that its kind of a generic
little piece of code you can cut and paste, and if you error great you
got an image to look at it.  If not it does nothing.

Like I said though this is a strategy well suited to local debugging,
and everything from there is a tad more nuanced.

On Thu, Mar 3, 2011 at 6:27 PM, Jeremiah Rounds

This is nice. The closest I came to was wrapping stuff
in tryCatch and saving the errors. But your code is cleaner.
(see [1]). be careful loading these saved environments, in case
map.values / map.keys is very large.

> Which raises the questions:
> 1) Does Rhipe kill a hadoop job on a map error(or does it have an
> option), and failing that,

If it's an R error it does indeed kill the job. Also it depends on how
large the input data is. If the data is small and the R error is
thrown after all the data has been read, the job dies only if rhstatus
is monitoring it from the R console (autokill=TRUE). Otherwise it runs
to the end, but the counters will have R_ERRORS in it.

 In other cases if an R error is thrown while hadoop is still reading
data then this error is converted to a Java exception and the job
fails. The source can be changed to not throw an exception (the Java
source which converts R errors to Java exceptions).

> 2) Is it possible to kill a hadoop job from inside a Rhipe map without
> knowing the ID of your job (I could add such a thing to the error
> function).

Throw an R error. If you're running rhstatus (from R command line) and
you throw an R error, it will kill the job.

What I don't know (haven't checked) is that if a job dies, will the
files copied to the output.folder (by copyFiles) remain or be removed
by Hadoop.

Regards
J

First, a caveat I have very little to basically no real experience

> R is that if you can avoid them you probably should. The reasons are
> they don't have good language tools for joining expressions, removing
> pieces of expressions, etc. Your options are to just cut and paste new
> and different expressions or to do some fairly opaque manipulations.
> Environments are a tad easier to manipulate.

Not sure about that.

x <- expression({ foo +1 })
as.list(x[[1]])

You can then swap in parts and modify expressions. Also, see [1]
for some examples of quote replacement.

However, I have spoken to some people and expressions are eschewed.

Also, I notice this

rhmrExtended.reduce$reduce()

If I create a variable in reduce$setup, using your approach
can i make persistant modifications in reduce$pre() and reduce$reduce()
so that e.g. reduce$post() will see them?

I think I made use of this somewhere in the manual. It is not a often
used construct, so if your method doesn't it's not a big deal.

We could include it.

Regards

Saptarshi

> So as an extensions to what I mentioned in a global setup thread, I
> thought about how I could do away with all the expressions.  And I
> came up with rhmrEx.  Ex stands for extended.  And the extension is to
> make the call check for function and environment arguments in map,
> reduce, and setup, and if those are detected it uses the setup as an
> environment scheme to create map and reduce expressions--thus hiding
> the details of expressions from would be Rhipe users.    If a map/
> reduce function has no arguments it is assumed to be aware of Rhipes
> global environment variables. If it has a single argument it assumes
> you want the values.  If it has two you are assumed to want
> key,values.  Environments are assumed to have functions with names
> like that for map and reduce expressions (eg pre/map/post).  The
> environment form of map and reduce operates just like the expression
> form in that regard except that everything in the map/reduce
> environments comes along for the ride for no extra work.    The code
> goes like this though it is really just a proof of concept rather than
> a formal submission.  I haven't extensively tested it, and these
> things being what they are I am sure it would break under some non-
> trivial uses. Note: one way is that the environments for map and
> reduce get attached before calling map and reduce functions.
> Depending on what is in those environments that could be an issue.
> Note: there is an attach in setup that never gets detached that causes
> warnings.
>
>
>
> The uses look like these.
> Worst count words ever:
> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> library(Rhipe)
> rhinit()
> source("rhmrExtended.R")
> #countWordsExample
> map = function(values){

>

> args$ofolder = paste(DIR,"output", sep="/")
> args$inout = c("text","text")
> args$mapred = list(mapred.job.tracker='local')
> mr = do.call("rhmrEx", args)
> rhex(mr)
> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Here is the get the airline data example.  This last example
> demonstrates the flexibility of thinking of map as an environment.
> Here we just say "oh lets just put wget in the map environment to go
> along for the ride."  And its as simple as that.
>
> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> library(Rhipe)
> rhinit(TRUE,TRUE)
> rhoptions(runner=sprintf("%s/rhipe.runner.sh <http://rhipe.runner.sh>",Sys.getenv("HOME")))
> source("rhmrExtended.R")
> wget = function(on){

>    on <- sprintf("http://stat-computing.org/dataexpo/
> 2009/%s.csv.bz2",x)

> # mc is call to rhmrExtended.

> # if setup is anything else it leaves it alone

> rhmrExtended.map$pre();  },

> >rhmrExtended.reduce$reduce()
> >If I create a variable in reduce$setup, using your approach

> >so that e.g. reduce$post() will see them?
>

> take it the issue is that there can be many different R instances
> between a pre call and a post call? Is that the issue?

I had come to terms with map operations and reduce operations, but not
pre and post yet. I think its the case in Rhipe that every key in
hadoop reduce for a single key gets its own R instance,  The pre
expression gets ran once before reducing and the post expression gets
ran once after keys are ran. The reduce expression is ran in a single
R instance multiple times if the size of value for a single key is
huge.

Assuming that is the case the question is about scope and not about
instances of R and machines etc.  So, yes there is the added
complication of a scope issue when using functions for map/reduce.
There are two ways to deal with the scope issue.
For example let us consider the code from [1] (not the hard code the
easy code used to demonstrate the hard code):

reduce <- expression(
    pre={ total <- 0},
    reduce = { total <- total+sum(unlist(reduce.values)) }
    post = { rhcollect(reduce.key,total) }
    )

The two ways that should do the same work (these are untested) (here
args is just my style of forming rhmr arguments prior to the call)

1) Use "<<-" to create and alter a variable in the global scope
(assuming it doesn't run into a variable with the same name sooner).
args = list()
args$reduce = new.env()
args$reduce$pre = function() { total <<- 0}
args$reduce$reduce = function() { total <<- total +
sum(unlist(reduce.values))}
args$reduce$post = function() {rhcollect(reduce.key, total)}

2) Add a working environment to the reduce environment and make
changes to it
args = list()
args$reduce = new.env()
args$reduce$working = new.env()
args$reduce$pre = function() {working$total = 0}
args$reduce$reduce = function() working$total = working$total +
sum(unlist(reduce.values))}
args$reduce$post = function() {rhcollect(reduce.key, working$total)}

If the issue is subtler than that then we have exposed something I
need to learn!  Thanks for the offer to consider adding it.  I got
some major Rhipe work coming. There is a good chance I will tweak as I
get experience.  This is just an idea, and some hours of chasing it.
In the end, the toughest selling point is there is nothing you can do
with environments that you can't do with expressions.

> I had come to terms with map operations and reduce operations, but not
> pre and post yet. I think its the case in Rhipe that every key in
> hadoop reduce for a single key gets its own R instance,  The pre
> expression gets ran once before reducing and the post expression gets
> ran once after keys are ran. The reduce expression is ran in a single
> R instance multiple times if the size of value for a single key is
> huge.

Nopes, for every /block/ of data there is an R instance. (Note, in the
JNI version (on github) you can have one jvm start which will process
a series of blocks, in this case one R instances trundles through
those blocks) So, when a JVM is assigned a new block (which could
contain thousands of key-value pairs), an R instance is started. For
the map: setup is called once, then the keys/values are buffered and
the map expressions is calle repeatedly till the key-values have been
processed. Once done, the cleanup/close is called.

For reduce: Each JVM is assigned a series of keys (and their
corresponding values) to process. R is started and the setup for
reduce is called The pre is called for each new key assigned to that
reducer (which depends on the partitioner) then the reduce is called
repeatedly and then post. Then back to pre for the next key. Finally
the cleanup/close is called.

So, if i create/load a data set in setup in Reduce it is visible to
all the subsequent keys. And loading a data set once is more
efficient. This holds true in your modification. However, I can change
a variable in pre and the pre for subsequent keys will pick this up
(and post and reduce). This can be used for say computing differences
or weird stuff (see manual) - admittely i doubt many will need this.

>    pre={ total <- 0},
>    reduce = { total <- total+sum(unlist(reduce.values)) }

>    )

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

A user asked the question (see end of email) and the following was my
response. Might be useful.

So Rhipe gets the subsets from Hadoop in a streaming fashion and hands
them over to R in groups of N(N=5,000 default, was 10K, but 5 is
faster ...). This is to enhance execution speed.

This has nothing to with blocksize.Each reducer is incharge of writing
its subsets to disks (78 reducers == part-r-0000{1..78}). These
subsets (also called key-values) are written to the part-r-* file. If
the part-r-* file is greater than a blocksize Hadoop internally breaks
it up into smaller blocks and redistributes blocks. This is
transparent to the user. So a part-r-* file can contain many thousands
of subsets.

(1) You might be aware that RHIPE forces subsets to be smaller than
128MB. This is independent of Hadoop and is a restriction of the
serialization of the format. /However/ this is convenient: a subset is
always in one file and never split acros blocks.

In hindsight, the 5K approach is bad. Why? In the text to data frame
conversion I did, we read in 5K lines, combined them as a data
frame and wrote them as a subset. In the input, each subset is a
single line. So while reading, Rhipe is given 5K subsets each one line
of text. In the output,each subset is a data frame of 5K rows. Call
this output B.

If B is now read with the default 5k, R is handed 5K subsets each a
data frame of 5K rows! Combining this into a data frame would be a
combined data frame of 250K rows.  Issues
- just getting this into R takes too much time, leave alone
  processing.
That is why you might see rhipe_map_buff_sizs set to 5 or 10. This
  makes it much faster to read. But it is a tedious approach since the
  user is expected to know tedious details of the input.

A better approach to be used in next version (when Doug creates a
Hadoop user) is to set rhipe_ map_buf_input to X megabytes. If this
were say 50MB, then when the input is text (each subset one line), R
would be given many thousands of lines. When the input is like B, R
would be automatically handed a smaller number of subsets. There would
be little need for the user to modify this.

I have digressed, but (1) answers your question. Because of the 128MB
subset (key or value) restriction, a subset is always in one block (no
need to read two blocks get a subset) as long the blocksize is greater
than 128MB (which it is). And that is the only relation between
subsets and block size.  There is no constraint on the total size of
all the subsets in one part-{r/m} file.

Hope this clarifies things
Cheers
Saptarshi

> In rhipe rhmr(), my understanding is the
> function reads 10,000 subsets in map step by default. We can set an option
> to change it to a smaller number. The total size of these subsets need to be
> smaller than a blocksize 128MB (in our cluster A) or 256MB (in our
> cluster B).
>
> I am wondering what is a good size for one subset and whether there is a way
> to see the size of one subset?

Follow up to Blocksize

Yes, the 5k thing is entirely  a computing/processing thing and
nothing to with saving/writing to disk.
Data is written in a streaming fashion, so even if the total size was
massive this would not be problem for writing to disk
since individual record (subset/key/value) is less than a blocksize.

In summary, if each  input and output subset were 64MB, and the
rhipe_map_buf were 5K

- 1. data can be read (its streaming) - no problem and then aggregated
into 5K and handed to R, read another 5K hand over to R, loop.
- 2. data can be written - no problem
- BUT, a list of 5K subsets each 64MB ... probably won't fit in
memory! So (1) will probably fail, and even if (1) passed, R would
fail but if R could manage such a humungous list
(2) will succeed.

Summary of Summary: , keep subsets small. compute across subsets.
